keyVerseText: And there was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very sore, so that the land of Egypt and all the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb לָהַהּ (lâhahh) stems from a primitive root meaning 'to burn,' which metaphorically conveys a state of intense internal agitation or exhaustion. This root sense enriches the common English glosses such as 'faint' or 'mad' by suggesting an overwhelming, consuming experience akin to burning out from frenzy or distress, rather than a mere physical collapse or mental confusion. Thus, the root implies a profound weakening or disturbance that affects the whole person or land.
usageInScripture: This word appears only twice in Scripture, yet its usage spans a spectrum from physical fainting to a figurative sense of madness or amazement. The top translations include 'fainted' and 'as a mad,' indicating that the verb can describe both a physical languishing and a state of mental or emotional frenzy. This range reveals a consistent theme of intense weakening or disturbance, whether bodily or psychologically, emphasizing the depth of distress involved.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding לָהַהּ in its original sense highlights the reality of human frailty and the profound effects of suffering and distress, whether physical or mental. The imagery of burning and languishing calls attention to the brokenness of creation under the curse of sin and the consequences of famine, despair, or madness. For the Christian faith, this word reminds us that God's people are vulnerable and in need of divine sustenance and restoration. It points forward to Christ as the one who revives the faint and brings sanity and healing to those overwhelmed by spiritual and physical exhaustion.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 47:13 states, 'And there was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very sore, so that the land of Egypt and all the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine.' Here, לָהַהּ vividly expresses the land's utter depletion and weakness caused by famine. The verb conveys not just a lack of food but an exhausted, burning out condition that affects the entire region, emphasizing the severity of the crisis and the vulnerability of God's people in times of trial.
